title: The mole, Avogadro's constant and relative masses
html:
Guiding question

How do we quantify matter on the atomic scale?

Atoms are far too small to count one by one and far too light to weigh individually. Chemists get round this the same way a bank counts banknotes: by weighing a large batch. If you know the mass of one note and the mass of the stack, you know how many notes there are without counting a single one. The mole is the "batch size" chemists use for particles.

CodeUnderstanding
S1.4.1The mole (mol) is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly the number of elementary entities given by the Avogadro constant.
S1.4.2Masses of atoms are compared on a scale relative to ¹²C and are expressed as relative atomic mass (Ar) and relative formula mass (Mr).
S1.4.3Molar mass (M) has the units g mol⁻¹.
S1.4.4The empirical formula gives the simplest ratio of atoms of each element in a compound; the molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule.
S1.4.5Molar concentration is determined by the amount of solute and the volume of solution.
S1.4.6Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases measured at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

S1.4.1 The mole and the Avogadro constant

Even a balance reading to 0.0001 g cannot detect a single atom: one carbon atom has a mass of about 2 × 10⁻²³ g. But if we know the mass of a very large, fixed number of atoms, we can work back to the mass of one atom, and forward to the number of atoms in any sample we weigh.

  • The mole (mol) is the SI unit of amount of substance, symbol n.
  • One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities (the Avogadro constant, NA). Use 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ from section 2 of the data booklet.
  • A mole is just a counting word, like "a dozen" means 12. You could, in principle, have a mole of students (it would need a very large school).
  • Think of buying sweets by the tube rather than one at a time: a tube is a convenient "package" of a fixed number of sweets, just as a mole is a package of 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
  • The entity must always be stated: atoms, molecules, ions, formula units or electrons. "One mole of oxygen" is ambiguous; "one mole of O₂ molecules" is not.
  • Since 2018 the mole is defined by this fixed number, not as "the number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12". The difference is negligible for calculations.
N = n × NA     n = N ÷ NA
DefinitionAvogadro constant: the number of elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions…) in one mole of a substance, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Note the unit: mol⁻¹, because it is "particles per mole". (You may meet the claim that NA has no units because it is "just a number"; that is true of the Avogadro number, 6.02 × 10²³, but the Avogadro constant always carries mol⁻¹.)
Worked example · atoms inside moleculesHow many oxygen atoms are in 2.00 mol of O₂?
Molecules: N = 2.00 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.20 × 10²⁴ O₂ molecules.
Each molecule contains 2 O atoms, so N(O) = 2 × 1.20 × 10²⁴ = 2.41 × 10²⁴ atoms.
Worked example · from particles to molesWhat amount of O₂ contains 1.8 × 10²² molecules?
n = 1.8 × 10²² ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 0.030 mol (2 s.f., matching the data).
Common mistakeCounting the wrong entity. One mole of ethanol, C₂H₅OH, contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules but 6 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.61 × 10²⁴ hydrogen atoms. One mole of NaCl contains 2 × 6.02 × 10²³ ions (Na⁺ and Cl⁻). Always multiply by the number of the particle you are asked about.

What is the number of atoms of oxygen in 2.0 mol of hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O? (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)

  1. 6
  2. 26
  3. 3.6 × 10²⁴
  4. 1.6 × 10²⁵

Each formula unit has 3 O (carbonate) + 10 O (water) = 13 O atoms. 2.0 mol × 13 = 26 mol of O atoms; 26 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.6 × 10²⁵. "26" is the amount in moles, not the number of atoms.

How many atoms of nitrogen are there in 0.50 mol of (NH₄)₂CO₃?

  1. 1
  2. 2
  3. 3.01 × 10²³
  4. 6.02 × 10²³

There are 2 N per formula unit, so 0.50 × 2 = 1.0 mol N atoms = 6.02 × 10²³ atoms. 3.01 × 10²³ forgets the subscript 2 outside the bracket.

What amount (in mol) of hydrogen atoms is in 0.250 mol of methane, CH₄?

n(H) = 4 × 0.250 = 1.00 mol of H atoms, which is 1.00 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.

S1.4.2 Relative atomic mass and relative formula mass

Because atoms are so light, their masses are compared with a standard rather than quoted in grams. The standard is the carbon-12 atom, given a mass of exactly 12 units, so one unit is 1/12 of the mass of a ¹²C atom.

  • Relative atomic mass, Ar: the weighted average mass of the atoms of an element (taking all naturally occurring isotopes and their abundances into account) compared with 1/12 of the mass of one atom of carbon-12.
  • This is why chlorine has Ar = 35.45. You cannot have 0.45 of a proton; the value is an average of Cl-35 and Cl-37 (see S1.2).
  • Relative formula mass, Mr: the sum of the Ar values of all the atoms in the formula. For molecules it is also called relative molecular mass; for ionic compounds use the formula unit.
  • Ar and Mr are ratios, so they have no units.

Your teacher's picture for this is a flock of sheep: each atom is a sheep wearing a tag with its Ar. To find how "heavy" a molecule is, line up its sheep and add the tags.

Worked example · Mr values CO₂: 12.01 + 2 × 16.00 = 44.01
H₂SO₄: 2 × 1.01 + 32.07 + 4 × 16.00 = 98.09
Fe₂O₃: 2 × 55.85 + 3 × 16.00 = 159.70
KMnO₄: 39.10 + 54.94 + 4 × 16.00 = 158.04
Co₂(SO₄)₃: 2 × 58.93 + 3 × (32.07 + 4 × 16.00) = 406.07 — expand brackets carefully: everything inside is multiplied by 3.
Exam tipUse the data booklet Ar values to two decimal places (H = 1.01, C = 12.01, O = 16.00, Cl = 35.45). Mark schemes for multiple-choice usually do not penalise whole numbers, but Paper 2 answers can fall outside the accepted range if you round Ar or Mr too early.

Speed round: who can calculate these fastest?

Use data booklet Ar values. Type your answer to 2 d.p.

Mr of LiI

6.94 + 126.90 = 133.84

Mr of NH₃

14.01 + 3 × 1.01 = 17.04

Mr of MgCl₂

24.31 + 2 × 35.45 = 95.21

Mr of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆

6 × 12.01 + 12 × 1.01 + 6 × 16.00 = 72.06 + 12.12 + 96.00 = 180.18

Mr of Ni(CH₃CO₂)₂

Each ethanoate CH₃CO₂ contains 2 C, 3 H, 2 O; there are two of them: 58.69 + 4 × 12.01 + 6 × 1.01 + 4 × 16.00 = 58.69 + 48.04 + 6.06 + 64.00 = 176.79

Mr of Na₂HPO₄

2 × 22.99 + 1.01 + 30.97 + 4 × 16.00 = 141.96
More answers to check yourself (CH₄, CO₂, HCl, H₂SO₄, NaCl, TiO, Fe₂O₃, C₄H₁₀, MnO₄, C₆H₁₂, KMnO₄, Co₂(SO₄)₃)

CH₄ 16.05 · CO₂ 44.01 · HCl 36.46 · H₂SO₄ 98.09 · NaCl 58.44 · TiO 63.87 · Fe₂O₃ 159.70 · C₄H₁₀ 58.14 · MnO₄ 118.94 · C₆H₁₂ 84.18 · KMnO₄ 158.04 · Co₂(SO₄)₃ 406.07 (2 × 58.93 + 3 × 32.07 + 12 × 16.00).

Key terms

Fill the gaps: the SI unit of amount of substance is the mole, and atomic masses are measured relative to the isotope carbon-12.

title: Molar mass and mole calculations
html:
S1.4.3 Molar mass and the n = m/M triangle

Molar mass, M, is the mass of one mole of a substance in g mol⁻¹. It has the same number as Ar or Mr but, unlike them, it has units. M(CO₂) = 44.01 g mol⁻¹. This is the bridge between the balance and the particle world: 44.01 g of CO₂ on the balance contains 6.02 × 10²³ CO₂ molecules.

n = m ÷ M     m = n × M     M = m ÷ n

Cover the quantity you want in the "moles triangle" (m on top, n and M below) to see the rearrangement. The mass must be in grams (convert kg × 1000 first).

Worked example · mass to particlesHow many molecules are in 8.0 g of methane, CH₄?
M(CH₄) = 12.01 + 4 × 1.01 = 16.05 g mol⁻¹
n = 8.0 ÷ 16.05 = 0.50 mol
N = 0.50 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.0 × 10²³ molecules
Worked example · identifying an unknown from M0.502 g of a Group 1 sulfate, X₂SO₄, gives 0.672 g of BaSO₄ precipitate with excess BaCl₂(aq).
n(BaSO₄) = 0.672 ÷ 233.40 = 2.88 × 10⁻³ mol = n(X₂SO₄) (one sulfate each)
M(X₂SO₄) = 0.502 ÷ 2.88 × 10⁻³ = 174 g mol⁻¹
2Ar(X) = 174 − 96.07 = 78 → Ar(X) ≈ 39 → potassium.
Common mistakeWriting units on Ar or Mr, or leaving them off M. "Which quantity has units: Ar, Mr, molar mass or mass number?" is a favourite multiple-choice question. Answer: molar mass only.

Which of the following quantities has units?

  1. Relative atomic mass
  2. Relative molecular mass
  3. Molar mass
  4. Mass number

Molar mass is a mass per mole (g mol⁻¹). Ar and Mr are ratios to 1/12 of a ¹²C atom, and mass number is a count of nucleons, so none of those has units.

Moles questions

Work these out, then check. Use data booklet Ar values.

Calculate the mass of 0.100 mol of lithium metal.

m = n × M = 0.100 × 6.94 = 0.694 g

Calculate the mass of 0.200 mol of sodium bromide, NaBr.

M(NaBr) = 22.99 + 79.90 = 102.89 g mol⁻¹; m = 0.200 × 102.89 = 20.6 g

Calculate the amount (mol) in 0.150 g of iron.

n = 0.150 ÷ 55.85 = 2.69 × 10⁻³ mol

Calculate the amount (mol) in 1.23 g of Na₂SO₄.

M = 2 × 22.99 + 32.07 + 4 × 16.00 = 142.05 g mol⁻¹; n = 1.23 ÷ 142.05 = 8.66 × 10⁻³ mol

0.107 mol of an element X has a mass of 13.59 g. Calculate its molar mass.

M = m ÷ n = 13.59 ÷ 0.107 = 127 g mol⁻¹, so X is iodine (Ar 126.90).

How many moles of H atoms are there in 98.1 g of H₂SO₄?

n(H₂SO₄) = 98.1 ÷ 98.09 = 1.00 mol. Each H₂SO₄ has 2 H, so n(H) = 2.00 mol. (The same sample contains 1.00 mol of SO₄²⁻.)

How many moles are present in 34 g of Cu(OH)₂?

M = 63.55 + 2 × 17.01 = 97.57 g mol⁻¹; n = 34 ÷ 97.57 = 0.35 mol

What is the mass of 4.2 mol of Ca(NO₃)₂?

M = 40.08 + 2 × (14.01 + 3 × 16.00) = 164.10 g mol⁻¹; m = 4.2 × 164.10 = 689 g (6.9 × 10² g to 2 s.f.)
How are "molar mass" and "relative atomic mass" different? Predict, then reveal.

Relative atomic mass compares the average mass of an atom with 1/12 of a ¹²C atom and has no units. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance (element or compound) and has units of g mol⁻¹. For an element the two have the same number: Ar(Mg) = 24.31, M(Mg) = 24.31 g mol⁻¹.

Exam practice

What is the molar mass, in g mol⁻¹, of a compound if 0.200 mol of the compound has a mass of 13.2 g?

  1. 66.0
  2. 66
  3. 26.4
  4. 26

M = 13.2 ÷ 0.200 = 66.0 g mol⁻¹. Both data values have 3 s.f., so the answer is given to 3 s.f. (66.0, not 66). 26.4 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

What is the number of carbon atoms in 12 g of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH (Mr = 60)?

  1. 0.20
  2. 2.0
  3. 1.2 × 10²³
  4. 2.4 × 10²³

n = 12 ÷ 60 = 0.20 mol of molecules. Each has 2 C atoms → 0.40 mol C = 0.40 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 2.4 × 10²³. 1.2 × 10²³ is the number of molecules, not C atoms.

Which contains the greatest number of moles of oxygen atoms?

  1. 0.05 mol Mg(NO₃)₂
  2. 0.05 mol C₆H₄(NO₂)₂
  3. 0.1 mol H₂O
  4. 0.1 mol NO₂

Count O per formula: Mg(NO₃)₂ has 6 → 0.30 mol; C₆H₄(NO₂)₂ has 4 → 0.20 mol; H₂O has 1 → 0.10 mol; NO₂ has 2 → 0.20 mol.

Which compound has the greatest percentage by mass of nitrogen?

  1. N₂H₄
  2. NH₃
  3. N₂O₄
  4. NaNO₃

N₂H₄: 28.02 ÷ 32.06 = 87%. NH₃: 82%. N₂O₄: 30%. NaNO₃: 16%. Hydrogen is so light that the N–H compounds are mostly nitrogen by mass.

title: Equations, reacting masses and limiting reactants
html:
Using moles with equations: balancing, reacting masses and limiting reactants

Molar mass lets us convert grams into moles. The balanced equation then tells us how many moles react with how many. Put the two together and you can predict the mass of any product from the mass of any reactant. (This is developed further in Reactivity 2.1; it is introduced here because every S1.4 calculation relies on it.)

Balancing equations

Example: aluminium burns in air to form aluminium oxide.

  1. Write the word equation: aluminium + oxygen → aluminium oxide.
  2. Write the correct formulas: Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃.
  3. Balance O: 2 O on the left, 3 on the right; the lowest common multiple is 6 → Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃.
  4. Re-balance Al: 4 on the right → 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃.
  5. Check every element: Al 4 = 4, O 6 = 6. Balanced.
Key point · tips for balancing
  1. Never change the subscripts in a formula to make it balance; only change coefficients.
  2. Leave elements that appear in several places (often O and H) until last.
  3. If it takes a huge number of steps, check that your formulas are right.
  4. In ionic equations the total charge must also balance.
  5. Finish by checking every element on both sides.
Try these, then reveal: (a) Fe + Cl₂ → FeCl₃ (b) Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃ (c) FeBr₃ + H₂SO₄ → Fe₂(SO₄)₃ + HBr (d) C₂H₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (e) NH₃ + O₂ → NO + H₂O

(a) 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃
(b) 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃
(c) 2FeBr₃ + 3H₂SO₄ → Fe₂(SO₄)₃ + 6HBr
(d) C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O
(e) 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O

Ionic example: Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl (1 : 1 : 1, not 2 : 2 : 1 — charges and atoms both balance with all coefficients equal to 1).

What is the sum of the coefficients when this equation is balanced with the lowest whole numbers? __Na₂S₂O₃(aq) + __HCl(aq) → __S(s) + __SO₂(g) + __NaCl(aq) + __H₂O(l)

  1. 6
  2. 7
  3. 8
  4. 9

Na₂S₂O₃ + 2HCl → S + SO₂ + 2NaCl + H₂O: 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 8.

What is the sum of the integer coefficients when propene burns completely? __C₃H₆ + __O₂ → __CO₂ + __H₂O

  1. 11
  2. 17
  3. 21
  4. 23

2C₃H₆ + 9O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O: 2 + 9 + 6 + 6 = 23. (With 1 C₃H₆ you would need 4½ O₂, so double everything to get whole numbers.)

What is the sum of the coefficients for __C₈H₁₈ + __O₂ → __CO + __H₂O (incomplete combustion)?

  1. 26.5
  2. 30
  3. 53
  4. 61

2C₈H₁₈ + 17O₂ → 16CO + 18H₂O: 2 + 17 + 16 + 18 = 53. 26.5 is the sum with a half-coefficient, which is not allowed.

What a balanced equation means

Use the mole ratios: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O. How much O₂ and Na₂O go with 12 mol Na? With 0.1 mol Na?

Ratio 4 : 1 : 2. 12 mol Na → 3 mol O₂ and 6 mol Na₂O. 0.1 mol Na → 0.025 mol O₂ and 0.05 mol Na₂O.

Similarly, for C₄H₁₀ + 6½O₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O, 0.5 mol butane gives 2 mol CO₂ and 2.5 mol H₂O, using 3.25 mol O₂.

Reacting-mass calculations: the moles method

Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂: starting with 24 g of magnesium (about 1 mol) we make about 120 g of MgSO₄ (1 mol). The same logic works for any masses if we go through moles.

  1. Balance the equation.
  2. Identify what you know and what you want to know.
  3. Convert the mass you know to moles using M.
  4. Use the mole ratio to find the moles of what you want.
  5. Convert moles to mass using M.
Worked example · fireworksWhat mass of KNO₃ is needed to make 1.6 g of O₂? 2KNO₃ → 2KNO₂ + O₂
n(O₂) = 1.6 ÷ 32.00 = 0.050 mol → n(KNO₃) = 2 × 0.050 = 0.10 mol
M(KNO₃) = 39.10 + 14.01 + 48.00 = 101.11 g mol⁻¹ → m = 0.10 × 101.11 = 10.1 g

Phosphorus reacts with chlorine: 2P + 3Cl₂ → 2PCl₃. Calculate the maximum mass of PCl₃ that can be made from 0.93 g of phosphorus.

n(P) = 0.93 ÷ 30.97 = 0.0300 mol; ratio P : PCl₃ = 2 : 2 = 1 : 1 → n(PCl₃) = 0.0300 mol; M(PCl₃) = 30.97 + 3 × 35.45 = 137.32 g mol⁻¹; m = 0.0300 × 137.32 = 4.12 g

What mass of magnesium oxide forms from the complete combustion of 6.0 g of magnesium? 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

n(Mg) = 6.0 ÷ 24.31 = 0.247 mol = n(MgO) (2 : 2); m = 0.247 × 40.31 = 9.95 g (≈ 10 g; whole-number Ar values give exactly 10 g).

What mass of copper can be obtained from 15.9 g of copper(II) oxide? CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O

n(CuO) = 15.9 ÷ 79.55 = 0.200 mol = n(Cu); m = 0.200 × 63.55 = 12.7 g

How much iron is needed to make 4.4 g of iron(II) sulfide? Fe + S → FeS

n(FeS) = 4.4 ÷ 87.92 = 0.0500 mol = n(Fe); m = 0.0500 × 55.85 = 2.8 g
Blast furnace: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. (a) Mass of Fe₂O₃ to make 112 g of Fe? (b) Iron from 320 tonnes of Fe₂O₃? (c) 320 t of an impure ore gives 202 t of iron. Percentage purity?

(a) n(Fe) = 112 ÷ 55.85 = 2.01 mol → n(Fe₂O₃) = 1.00 mol → 1.00 × 159.70 = 160 g.
(b) Tonnes behave like grams in the ratio: 320 ÷ 159.70 = 2.00 "tonne-moles" → 4.01 × 55.85 = 224 t.
(c) Pure Fe₂O₃ would give 224 t, so purity = 202 ÷ 224 × 100 = 90.3%.

Limiting and excess reactants

Often one reactant is present in more than the equation needs. The reactant that runs out first is the limiting reactant: it decides how much product forms. The other is in excess, and some of it is left over.

To find the limiting reactant, calculate the moles of each reactant and compare with the mole ratio in the equation. A quick test: divide each amount by its coefficient; the smallest result is the limiting reactant.

Worked example · ethane combustion15 g of C₂H₆ reacts with 45 g of O₂: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. What mass of water forms?
n(C₂H₆) = 15 ÷ 30.08 = 0.499 mol; n(O₂) = 45 ÷ 32.00 = 1.41 mol
To burn 0.499 mol C₂H₆ needs 0.499 × 7/2 = 1.75 mol O₂, but only 1.41 mol is present → O₂ is limiting.
n(H₂O) = 1.41 × 6/7 = 1.21 mol → m = 1.21 × 18.02 = 21.7 g
Common mistakeUsing the coefficient when calculating M: "4FeCl₃" does not mean M = 4 × 162.20. M is always for one formula unit; the coefficient is used only in the mole-ratio step. And you must find the limiting reactant before calculating the product.

6.0 g of FeCl₃ reacts with 4.0 g of O₂: 4FeCl₃ + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 6Cl₂. How many moles of Cl₂ form?

n(FeCl₃) = 6.0 ÷ 162.20 = 0.0370 mol; n(O₂) = 4.0 ÷ 32.00 = 0.125 mol. 0.125 mol O₂ would need 0.125 × 4/3 = 0.167 mol FeCl₃, more than we have, so O₂ is in excess and FeCl₃ is limiting. n(Cl₂) = 0.0370 × 6/4 = 0.0555 mol.

15.3 g of NaCl reacts with 60.8 g of Pb(NO₃)₂: 2NaCl + Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2NaNO₃ + PbCl₂. What mass of PbCl₂ forms?

n(NaCl) = 15.3 ÷ 58.44 = 0.262 mol; n(Pb(NO₃)₂) = 60.8 ÷ 331.22 = 0.184 mol. 0.184 mol Pb(NO₃)₂ would need 0.367 mol NaCl, so NaCl is limiting. n(PbCl₂) = 0.262 ÷ 2 = 0.131 mol; m = 0.131 × 278.1 = 36.4 g. Excess Pb(NO₃)₂ left = (0.184 − 0.131) × 331.22 = 17.4 g.

2Al + 6HBr → 2AlBr₃ + 3H₂. 3.22 mol Al reacts with 4.96 mol HBr. How many moles of H₂ form?

  1. 4.83 mol, Al limiting
  2. 2.48 mol, HBr limiting
  3. 4.83 mol, HBr limiting
  4. 2.48 mol, Al limiting

From Al: 3.22 × 3/2 = 4.83 mol H₂. From HBr: 4.96 × 3/6 = 2.48 mol H₂. The smaller amount wins, so HBr is limiting and 2.48 mol H₂ forms.

CO₂ + 3H₂ → CH₃OH + H₂O. What is the maximum amount of methanol from 2 mol CO₂ and 3 mol H₂?

  1. 1 mol
  2. 2 mol
  3. 3 mol
  4. 5 mol

3 mol H₂ is enough for only 1 mol CO₂ (1 : 3), so H₂ is limiting and 1 mol CH₃OH forms.

4FeS₂ + 11O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 8SO₂. 26.62 g FeS₂ reacts with 5.44 g O₂. Mass of SO₂? Predict, then reveal.

n(FeS₂) = 26.62 ÷ 119.99 = 0.222 mol → could make 0.444 mol SO₂.
n(O₂) = 5.44 ÷ 32.00 = 0.170 mol → could make 0.170 × 8/11 = 0.124 mol SO₂.
O₂ is limiting: m(SO₂) = 0.124 × 64.07 = 7.92 g. (Rounding to 0.12 mol and M = 64 too early gives 7.68 g, outside the accepted range.)

3FeCl₂ + 2Na₃PO₄ → Fe₃(PO₄)₂ + 6NaCl. 23 g FeCl₂ and 41 g Na₃PO₄. Limiting reagent, mass of NaCl, excess left, and % yield if 16.1 g NaCl is obtained?

n(FeCl₂) = 23 ÷ 126.75 = 0.181 mol; this needs 0.181 × 2/3 = 0.121 mol Na₃PO₄ = 19.8 g, and 41 g is available, so FeCl₂ is limiting.
n(NaCl) = 0.181 × 2 = 0.363 mol → 0.363 × 58.44 = 21.2 g.
Excess Na₃PO₄ = 41 − 19.8 = 21 g.
% yield = 16.1 ÷ 21.2 × 100 = 76%.

title: Water of crystallisation and hydrate practicals
html:
Water of crystallisation (hydrates)

Many salts trap water molecules in their crystal lattice: this is water of crystallisation. The dot in CuSO₄·5H₂O means five water molecules per formula unit. The water is loosely bound to the ions; for calculations we only need the ratio. Heating drives off the water and leaves the anhydrous salt.

  1. Mass of water = mass of hydrated salt − mass of anhydrous salt.
  2. Moles of anhydrous salt and moles of water (M(H₂O) = 18.02).
  3. Divide by the smaller to find x in salt·xH₂O.
Worked example · barium chloride hydrate5.00 g of BaCl₂·xH₂O leaves 4.26 g of anhydrous BaCl₂ after heating.
m(H₂O) = 5.00 − 4.26 = 0.74 g
n(BaCl₂) = 4.26 ÷ 208.23 = 0.0205 mol; n(H₂O) = 0.74 ÷ 18.02 = 0.0411 mol
Ratio 1 : 2.0 → BaCl₂·2H₂O
Worked example · using MrCaSO₄·xH₂O has Mr = 172. 136.15 + 18.02x = 172 → x = 1.99 ≈ 2.

A 1.98 g sample of a cobalt(II) chloride hydrate leaves 1.55 g of anhydrous CoCl₂ on heating. Find x in CoCl₂·xH₂O.

m(H₂O) = 1.98 − 1.55 = 0.43 g. n(CoCl₂) = 1.55 ÷ 129.83 = 0.0119 mol; n(H₂O) = 0.43 ÷ 18.02 = 0.0239 mol. Ratio 1 : 2.0 → CoCl₂·2H₂O.

A hydrate is 73.42% ammonium phosphate, (NH₄)₃PO₄, and 26.58% water by mass. Find x in (NH₄)₃PO₄·xH₂O.

M((NH₄)₃PO₄) = 3 × 18.05 + 30.97 + 64.00 = 149.12. n = 73.42 ÷ 149.12 = 0.492; n(H₂O) = 26.58 ÷ 18.02 = 1.475. Ratio 1 : 3.00 → (NH₄)₃PO₄·3H₂O, ammonium phosphate trihydrate.

52.0 g of hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·xH₂O, is made up to 5.00 dm³ of solution with concentration 0.0366 mol dm⁻³. Find x.

n = c × V = 0.0366 × 5.00 = 0.183 mol. M = 52.0 ÷ 0.183 = 284 g mol⁻¹. 284 − 105.99 = 178 → x = 178 ÷ 18.02 = 9.9 ≈ 10: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O (washing soda).

What is the value of x when 32.2 g of Na₂SO₄·xH₂O is heated, leaving 14.2 g of anhydrous Na₂SO₄? (Mr: H₂O = 18, Na₂SO₄ = 142)

  1. 0.1
  2. 1
  3. 5
  4. 10

n(Na₂SO₄) = 14.2 ÷ 142 = 0.100 mol; m(H₂O) = 18.0 g = 1.00 mol. Ratio 1 : 10 → x = 10. Option A is the inverted ratio.

Practical: the value of x in Epsom salts, MgSO₄·xH₂O

Epsom salts (used in bath salts, as a laxative and as a plant nutrient) are hydrated magnesium sulfate. Heating drives off the water: MgSO₄·xH₂O → MgSO₄ + xH₂O. Knowing the mass of the sample before heating and the mass of water lost, we can find x. The experiment uses the principle of heating to constant mass: as long as steam is still coming off, water is still being lost; once the mass stops decreasing, all the water has gone.

  1. Weigh an empty boiling tube (stand it in a beaker on the balance; use the same balance throughout).
  2. Add about 2 cm depth of hydrated magnesium sulfate and reweigh.
  3. Heat, holding the tube with a test-tube holder, cool and reweigh. Repeat until the mass is constant.

Risk assessment: hydrated magnesium sulfate is low hazard; the main risk is burns, so hold the tube with a holder, keep apparatus on a heatproof mat, move carefully with hot tubes, tie back hair, and wear eye protection.

Worked example · the model datan(MgSO₄) = 1.657 ÷ 120.38 = 0.01376 mol = n(MgSO₄·xH₂O)
M(hydrate) = 3.383 ÷ 0.01376 = 245.8 g mol⁻¹ → water part = 245.8 − 120.38 = 125.4
x = 125.4 ÷ 18.02 = 6.96 ≈ 7 → MgSO₄·7H₂O
Check with water moles: 1.726 ÷ 18.02 = 0.0958 mol; 0.0958 ÷ 0.01376 = 6.96 ✓
Practical · evaluating uncertainty
  • Balance to 0.01 g: each reading ±0.005 g; a mass found by difference uses two readings. For the smallest mass (1.657 g): 2 × 0.005 ÷ 1.657 × 100 = 0.60%.
  • Accepted M(MgSO₄·7H₂O) = 120.38 + 7 × 18.02 = 246.52. Experimental error = (246.52 − 245.8) ÷ 246.52 × 100 ≈ 0.3%. This is smaller than the apparatus uncertainty, so the result is accurate within the limits of the equipment.
  • A balance reading to 0.01 g is enough here: because x must be an integer, a ~0.6% uncertainty is acceptable, whereas a 0.1 g balance would give ~6% uncertainty. A 0.001 g balance is unnecessary for the same reason.
  • If the salt is not fully dehydrated, the mass of water is too small and x comes out too low. If it is overheated and decomposes, x comes out too high.

Why would a balance reading to 0.1 g be unsuitable for the Epsom salts experiment?

  1. It cannot weigh hot boiling tubes
  2. Its percentage uncertainty would be about 6%, too large to fix x as an integer
  3. It reads systematically too high
  4. Water would condense on it

±0.05 g per reading, two readings, on ~1.7 g gives 2 × 0.05 ÷ 1.657 × 100 ≈ 6%. That is enough to blur x = 7 into 6.5–7.4, so the integer cannot be fixed confidently.

Exam question: barium chloride hydrate

(a) What further work is needed in trial 2? (b) In trial 3 the crucible turned black outside. Cause, and effect on x? (c) Two assumptions? Reveal the mark-scheme points.

(a) The two masses in trial 2 (22.080 g and 21.865 g) do not agree, so water is still present: heat, cool and reweigh again until the mass is constant.
(b) Soot (carbon) from incomplete combustion, e.g. the Bunsen air hole closed (yellow flame). Soot adds mass after heating, so the mass of water appears smaller and x comes out lower.
(c) Any two: all the mass lost is water; all the water of crystallisation is lost; BaCl₂ does not decompose or react with air on heating; the crucible does not gain or lose mass; the anhydrous salt does not reabsorb water while cooling.

title: Molar concentration, standard solutions and dilution
html:
S1.4.5 Molar concentration

  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent; (aq) means water is the solvent.
  • Molar concentration = amount of solute ÷ volume of solution (not volume of solvent).
c = n ÷ V     units: mol dm⁻³ (V in dm³)
  • 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1 L. To convert cm³ to dm³, divide by 1000.
  • Mass concentration in g dm⁻³ = mass of solute ÷ volume. Convert with: g dm⁻³ = mol dm⁻³ × M.
  • Square brackets mean concentration in mol dm⁻³: [H⁺], [NaCl].
  • Parts per million (ppm) is used for very dilute solutions. For dilute aqueous solutions, 1 ppm ≈ 1 mg dm⁻³. So 1.25 g dm⁻³ = 1250 mg dm⁻³ ≈ 1250 ppm, and 0.5 mg cm⁻³ = 500 mg dm⁻³ ≈ 500 ppm.
Worked example · two-step concentrationCalculate the concentration of 47.5 g KMnO₄ in 250 cm³ of solution.
n = 47.5 ÷ 158.04 = 0.301 mol; V = 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.250 dm³
c = 0.301 ÷ 0.250 = 1.20 mol dm⁻³
Worked example · mass neededWhat mass of NaCl is needed for 250 cm³ of 1.50 mol dm⁻³ solution?
n = c × V = 1.50 × 0.250 = 0.375 mol; m = 0.375 × 58.44 = 21.9 g

80 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved to make 1.00 dm³ of solution. What is its concentration?

n = 80 ÷ 40.00 = 2.0 mol; c = 2.0 ÷ 1.00 = 2.0 mol dm⁻³

1.5 mol of potassium iodide in 150 cm³ of solution. Concentration?

V = 0.150 dm³; c = 1.5 ÷ 0.150 = 10 mol dm⁻³

What volume of 2 mol dm⁻³ silver nitrate contains 0.5 mol AgNO₃? (in dm³)

V = n ÷ c = 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 dm³ (250 cm³)

1.5 g of KI in 150 cm³ of solution. Concentration in mol dm⁻³?

n = 1.5 ÷ 166.00 = 9.04 × 10⁻³ mol; c = 9.04 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.150 = 0.0602 mol dm⁻³

Mass of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, needed for 10 cm³ of 0.4 mol dm⁻³ solution?

n = 0.4 × 0.010 = 0.004 mol; M(Na₂CO₃) = 105.99; m = 0.424 g. (Watch the formula: sodium carbonate is Na₂CO₃, not NaCO₃.)

Mass of MgSO₄ needed for 500 cm³ of 5 mol dm⁻³ solution?

n = 5 × 0.500 = 2.5 mol; M(MgSO₄) = 120.38; m = 2.5 × 120.38 = 301 g

Which solution contains the greatest amount (in mol) of solute?

  1. 10.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ NaCl
  2. 20.0 cm³ of 0.400 mol dm⁻³ NaCl
  3. 30.0 cm³ of 0.300 mol dm⁻³ NaCl
  4. 40.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ NaCl

n = cV: A 5.0, B 8.0, C 9.0, D 8.0 (× 10⁻³ mol). The most concentrated solution is not necessarily the one with the most solute.

A solution has a concentration of 1.25 g dm⁻³. What is this in ppm?

1.25 g = 1250 mg, so 1250 mg dm⁻³ ≈ 1250 ppm.

Standard solutions

A standard solution has an accurately known concentration. A primary standard is a solid that can be weighed out to make one directly: it must be very pure (about 99.9%), have a high molar mass (so weighing errors are relatively small), be stable and unreactive, and not absorb water or CO₂ from the air. A secondary standard (e.g. NaOH(aq), which absorbs CO₂ and water) is standardised by titration against a primary standard, and can then itself be used to analyse other solutions.

Practical · making a standard solution
  1. Weigh the solute accurately (at least 2 d.p.), ideally by difference.
  2. Dissolve it in a small volume of distilled water in a beaker, stirring.
  3. Transfer through a funnel into a volumetric flask.
  4. Rinse the beaker, rod and funnel with distilled water into the flask so no solute is lost.
  5. Make up to the graduation mark with distilled water, reading the bottom of the meniscus at eye level (add the last drops with a dropping pipette).
  6. Stopper and invert several times to mix.
Glassware choice: volumetric flasks and pipettes are far more precise than beakers or measuring cylinders.

Why must a primary standard have a high molar mass?

  1. So it dissolves faster
  2. So that a larger mass is weighed for a given amount, making the percentage weighing error smaller
  3. So it does not react with air
  4. So its solutions are coloured

The balance uncertainty is fixed (e.g. ±0.005 g), so weighing a bigger mass gives a smaller percentage uncertainty in the moles.

Dilution

Adding solvent changes the volume but not the amount of solute, so nbefore = nafter:

c₁V₁ = c₂V₂     volume of water added = V₂ − V₁
Worked example · final volume and water added10.0 cm³ of 1.5 mol dm⁻³ HCl is diluted to 0.10 mol dm⁻³.
V₂ = 1.5 × 10.0 ÷ 0.10 = 150 cm³ (final volume)
Water to add = 150 − 10.0 = 140 cm³
Worked example · adding water200 cm³ of water is added to 300 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ NaCl.
V₂ = 300 + 200 = 500 cm³; c₂ = 2.0 × 300 ÷ 500 = 1.2 mol dm⁻³
Common mistakeUsing the volume of water added as V₂. V₂ is the total final volume. Also check the unit of your answer: a concentration is in mol dm⁻³, not dm³.

What volume of water must be added to 0.5 mol dm⁻³ HCl to make 400 cm³ of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ HCl? (in cm³)

V₁ = c₂V₂ ÷ c₁ = 0.1 × 400 ÷ 0.5 = 80 cm³ of the stock acid. Water added = V₂ − V₁ = 400 − 80 = 320 cm³.

Solution stoichiometry (titrations)

Combine c = n/V with the mole ratio from the balanced equation (full detail in Reactivity 2.1). A mol – vol – conc table under the equation keeps the working tidy. In volumetric analysis a known volume of one solution is measured with a pipette into a conical flask, an indicator is added, and the other solution is added from a burette until the end point.

Worked example20.8 cm³ of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄ neutralises 25.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq). Find [NaOH].
H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
n(H₂SO₄) = 0.0500 × 0.0208 = 1.04 × 10⁻³ mol
n(NaOH) = 2 × 1.04 × 10⁻³ = 2.08 × 10⁻³ mol
[NaOH] = 2.08 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0832 mol dm⁻³
Worked example · finding x in a hydrate by titration4.29 g of Na₂CO₃·xH₂O is made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ portions need 15.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ HCl (Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + CO₂ + H₂O).
n(HCl) = 0.200 × 0.0150 = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol → n(Na₂CO₃) = 1.50 × 10⁻³ mol in 25.0 cm³
In 250 cm³: 1.50 × 10⁻² mol → M = 4.29 ÷ 0.0150 = 286 g mol⁻¹
286 − 105.99 = 180 → x = 180 ÷ 18.02 = 10

What volume of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl neutralises 25.0 cm³ of 0.160 mol dm⁻³ NaOH? (in cm³)

n(NaOH) = 0.160 × 0.0250 = 4.00 × 10⁻³ mol = n(HCl) (1 : 1). V = 4.00 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.100 = 0.0400 dm³ = 40.0 cm³.

500 cm³ of 10.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl is spilled. What mass of CaCO₃ neutralises it? 2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

n(HCl) = 10.0 × 0.500 = 5.00 mol → n(CaCO₃) = 2.50 mol → m = 2.50 × 100.09 = 250 g.

Assuming complete reaction, what volume of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ Ba(OH)₂(aq)?

  1. 12.5 cm³
  2. 25.0 cm³
  3. 50.0 cm³
  4. 75.0 cm³

Ba(OH)₂ + 2HCl → BaCl₂ + 2H₂O. n(Ba(OH)₂) = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol → n(HCl) = 1.00 × 10⁻² mol → 50.0 cm³. 25.0 cm³ ignores the 1 : 2 ratio.

Challenge: 1.25 g of impure NaOH is made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ needs 30.3 cm³ of 0.102 mol dm⁻³ HCl. Percentage purity?

n(HCl) = 0.102 × 0.0303 = 3.09 × 10⁻³ mol = n(NaOH) in 25.0 cm³ → 3.09 × 10⁻² mol in 250 cm³ → m = 3.09 × 10⁻² × 40.00 = 1.24 g. Purity = 1.24 ÷ 1.25 × 100 = 98.9%.

Calibration curves

Make a series of standard solutions (by serial dilution), measure a property that depends on concentration (absorbance in a colorimeter, conductivity, pH), and plot property against concentration. Read off the unknown's concentration from its measured value. The curve should be linear through the origin in the working range; dilute the unknown if it falls outside the standards, then multiply back by the dilution factor.

Fill the gap: in c₁V₁ = c₂V₂, V₂ is the total volume after dilution.

title: Avogadro's law and problem-solving summary
html:
S1.4.6 Avogadro's law

DefinitionAvogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases, measured at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules (particles).

Why should this be true for every gas, whatever the size of its molecules? In a gas the particles are very far apart, so the volume is almost entirely empty space. The volume therefore depends on how many particles there are (and on T and p), not on what they are.

V ∝ n  (constant T, p)     n₁ ÷ V₁ = n₂ ÷ V₂
  • For reacting gases at the same T and p, the volume ratio equals the mole ratio in the balanced equation. You can work in volumes directly without converting to moles.
  • It applies to gases only. Ignore liquids and solids (e.g. H₂O(l)) when comparing volumes.
  • Doubling the amount of gas at constant T and p doubles the volume: 0.50 mol N₂ in 10.0 dm³ becomes 20.0 dm³ when the amount rises to 1.0 mol. This matters in industrial gas storage: the volume (or, at fixed volume, the pressure) of a cylinder rises in direct proportion to the gas added.
  • At STP (273.15 K, 100 kPa) one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.7 dm³ (see S1.5).
Worked example · limiting gas volume20.0 dm³ of propane reacts with 120.0 dm³ of oxygen: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g).
20.0 dm³ propane needs 5 × 20.0 = 100.0 dm³ O₂, so O₂ is in excess by 20.0 dm³.
Products: CO₂ = 3 × 20.0 = 60.0 dm³; H₂O(g) = 4 × 20.0 = 80.0 dm³.
Worked example3.0 dm³ SO₂ reacts with 2.0 dm³ O₂: 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃. 3.0 dm³ SO₂ needs only 1.5 dm³ O₂, so SO₂ is limiting and 3.0 dm³ SO₃ forms (0.5 dm³ O₂ left over).
Common mistakeAdding the reactant volumes to get the product volume (3.0 + 2.0 = 5.0 dm³ SO₃). Gas volumes are not conserved — moles of gas can change in a reaction. Only the ratio from the equation counts.

3.0 dm³ of SO₂ reacts with 2.0 dm³ of O₂: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g). What volume of SO₃ forms (same T and p)?

  1. 5.0 dm³
  2. 4.0 dm³
  3. 3.0 dm³
  4. 2.0 dm³

SO₂ is limiting (it needs only 1.5 dm³ of the 2.0 dm³ O₂). SO₂ : SO₃ = 2 : 2, so 3.0 dm³ SO₃.

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). What volume of ammonia forms from 25 dm³ of N₂ and 60 dm³ of H₂ (same T and p, complete reaction)?

  1. 40 dm³
  2. 50 dm³
  3. 85 dm³
  4. 120 dm³

60 dm³ H₂ needs only 20 dm³ N₂, so H₂ is limiting. NH₃ = 60 × 2/3 = 40 dm³. 50 dm³ assumes N₂ is limiting.

What volume of oxygen reacts with 0.40 dm³ of ethyne? 2C₂H₂(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)

Volume ratio C₂H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 5, so V(O₂) = 0.40 × 5/2 = 1.0 dm³.
A 10.0 dm³ container holds 0.50 mol N₂. More N₂ is added until there is 1.0 mol, at constant T and p. New volume? Predict, then reveal.

V ∝ n, so doubling n doubles V: V₂ = 10.0 × 1.0 ÷ 0.50 = 20.0 dm³.

Problem-solving summary

You knowUseTo get
number of particles Nn = N ÷ NAamount n
mass m (g)n = m ÷ Mamount n
c and V (dm³) of a solutionn = c × Vamount n
volume of gas at STPn = V ÷ 22.7amount n
p, V, T of a gasn = pV ÷ RTamount n
amount of Amole ratio from equationamount of B
Exam tipAlmost every calculation goes "convert to moles → use the ratio → convert out of moles". Keep unrounded values in your calculator, round only the final answer, and give it to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data value.
Linking questionsS3.1 — Atoms increase in mass down the periodic table; which properties follow this trend? R2.1 — How are molar masses used with equations to find masses of products? S3.2 — How does combustion analysis help identify an organic compound?
